subject: Anthropology
title: Fictive Kinship
description: A micro-lesson that makes Fictive Kinship usable.

hook.text: She calls her mother's friend 'auntie.' He calls his gang members 'brothers.' No blood ties, but real family bonds.

buildup.text: Fictive kinship creates family-like bonds between people who are not related by blood or marriage.

discovery.text: Godparents, blood brothers, and chosen families are all forms of fictive kinship found across many cultures worldwide.

twist.text: Fictive kin often carry real duties. A godparent may be obligated to raise a child if the parents die.

climax.text: Fictive kinship shows that family is a social creation. Bonds of choice can be as strong as bonds of biology.

punchline.text: Chosen family is still real family.

quiz.question: What is fictive kinship?
options: Family-like bonds between people not related by blood or marriage

details.summary: Fictive kinship creates family-like bonds between people who are not related by blood or marriage. Godparenthood, blood brotherhood, and chosen family networks demonstrate that kinship can be deliberately constructed through social choice and ritual.
details.whyItMatters: Fictive kinship shows that family is not limited to biology. Societies have always created mechanisms for turning strangers into family, expanding support networks and social bonds beyond the constraints of birth and marriage.
takeaways: Fictive kinship creates family bonds without biological connection
Examples include godparenthood, blood brotherhood, and chosen family
It demonstrates that kinship is socially constructed, not just biological

faq.question: What are common examples of fictive kinship?
faq.answer: Godparenthood in Latin American compadrazgo systems creates lifelong bonds between families. Blood brotherhood in many African societies creates kinship through ritual. LGBTQ+ chosen family networks and gang families also represent fictive kinship in modern contexts.

faq.question: Why is fictive kinship important for marginalized groups?
faq.answer: People excluded from biological family support — through migration, discrimination, or estrangement — rely on fictive kinship for mutual aid, emotional support, and social identity. LGBTQ+ chosen families are a well-documented modern example of this survival strategy.
